title: Homeostasis: how your body keeps its warmth and water steady

summary.text: On a hot May afternoon and on a cold winter morning, the inside of your body stays at about 37 degrees. Keeping the inside steady like this is called homeostasis. When you get hot, you sweat, and the drying sweat carries heat away. When you get cold, you shiver, and your working muscles make heat. When you are low on water, you feel thirsty. A small part of your brain, the hypothalamus, keeps checking and correcting all of this, day and night.
summary.art: A child in the middle of a see-saw: on one side a blazing sun and a sweating face, on the other a snowflake and a shivering child, with a small dial in the middle pointing to 'just right'.

intro.hook: Put the back of your hand on your cheek. Now put it on a steel plate or a tile floor. Which feels warmer? The inside of your body stays about the same warmth in hot summer and cold winter. How does it do that?
intro.text: Think about the hottest day you remember, maybe in May. Now think about a cold winter morning, when you wanted to stay under the blanket. The air around you changed a lot between those two days. But the inside of your body stayed almost exactly the same warmth, about 37 degrees. A steel plate left in the sun gets hot. Left outside on a winter night, it gets cold. You are not like the plate. Something inside you keeps checking your warmth and fixing it. That checking and fixing has a name: homeostasis.
intro.art: Split picture: a steel plate glowing hot in the sun and frosty in winter, next to the same smiling child in both scenes with a small '37' badge on the chest.

outcomes: I can say what homeostasis means: my body keeping things like warmth and water just right.
I can explain how sweating cools me down and how shivering warms me up.
I can explain why I feel thirsty, and how my body keeps its water balanced.
I can describe a feedback loop: something notices a change, the brain decides, and the body acts to undo it.
I can run a fair test with two tumblers and a thermometer, and show my results in a table and a chart.
I can give examples of balance-keeping in animals, plants, the Earth and machines at home.
I can say what scientists agree on, and what they still do not know, like why we are about 37 degrees and how hot is too hot.

terms.meaning: Homeostasis means keeping the inside of your body steady and just right. Say it like this: ho-mee-oh-STAY-sis.
terms.example: Your body stays about 37 degrees warm, on a hot day and on a cold day.
terms.art: A child balancing on one foot with a dial on their chest pointing to 'just right'.

terms.meaning: Body temperature is how warm the inside of your body is.
terms.example: Most people are about 37 degrees inside. A fever is when it goes higher.
terms.art: A digital thermometer under a child's arm showing 36.8.

terms.meaning: A thermometer is a tool that measures how hot or cold something is.
terms.example: A doctor puts a thermometer under your arm or in your mouth.
terms.art: Three thermometers: a digital fever thermometer, a kitchen probe and a glass lab thermometer.

terms.meaning: Degrees Celsius are the units we use to measure warmth. We write them like this: °C.
terms.example: Water freezes at 0 degrees Celsius. You are about 37 degrees Celsius.
terms.art: A tall thermometer marked at 0 with an ice cube, 37 with a child, and 100 with a boiling pot.

terms.meaning: Sweat is the salty water your skin lets out when you are hot.
terms.example: After playing cricket in the sun, your forehead is wet with sweat.
terms.art: A child's forehead with tiny drops of sweat, a cricket bat in hand.

terms.meaning: A sweat gland is a tiny tube in your skin that makes sweat. You have millions of them.
terms.example: Your palms and the soles of your feet have lots of sweat glands.
terms.art: A zoomed-in slice of skin showing a coiled tube opening at a tiny pore.

terms.meaning: Evaporation is when a liquid slowly turns into a gas and goes into the air. It is how wet things dry.
terms.example: Wet clothes on the line dry because the water evaporates.
terms.art: Clothes on a washing line with wavy lines rising from them into the air.

terms.meaning: Shivering is when your muscles shake by themselves to make heat.
terms.example: Coming out of a cold river, your teeth chatter and your body shakes.
terms.art: A child wrapped in a towel by a river, teeth chattering, small shake lines around them.

terms.meaning: Goosebumps are little bumps on your skin. Tiny muscles pull each hair up straight when you are cold.
terms.example: When a cold wind blows on your arm, the hairs stand up.
terms.art: A close-up of an arm with small bumps and hairs standing up.

terms.meaning: Blood vessels are the tubes that carry blood around your body.
terms.example: When you are hot, the blood vessels near your skin open wide. That is why your cheeks go red.
terms.art: A child's red cheeks with a zoom circle showing wide tubes of blood under the skin.

terms.meaning: Thirst is the feeling that tells you that your body needs water.
terms.example: After running in the park, you want a big glass of water.
terms.art: A child gulping water from a steel tumbler after running.

terms.meaning: The hypothalamus is a small part of your brain, about the size of an almond. It watches your warmth and water and decides what to do.
terms.example: When your blood gets too warm, your hypothalamus tells your skin to sweat.
terms.art: A side view of a child's head with a small almond-shaped spot glowing deep in the middle of the brain.

terms.meaning: A set point is the 'just right' number your body tries to stay at.
terms.example: Your warmth set point is about 37 degrees. An AC also has a set point, like 26 degrees.
terms.art: An AC remote showing 26 next to a child with a dial showing 37.

terms.meaning: A feedback loop is a circle of steps. Something notices a change, something decides, and something acts to undo the change. Then it checks again.
terms.example: Too hot, so you sweat. You cool down, so the sweating stops.
terms.art: A circle of three arrows: a thermometer (notice), a brain (decide), a sweating face (act).

terms.meaning: A sensor is something that notices a change, like heat, cold or saltiness.
terms.example: Tiny nerve endings in your skin are sensors for hot and cold.
terms.art: Skin with tiny glowing nerve endings, one feeling a warm sun, one feeling an ice cube.

terms.meaning: Dehydration means your body has lost more water than you have drunk.
terms.example: On a long, hot bus trip with no water, you might feel tired, dizzy and have a headache.
terms.art: A tired child in a hot bus, with an empty water bottle.

terms.meaning: Humidity is how much water is already in the air.
terms.example: Mumbai in the monsoon is very humid. Wet clothes take ages to dry.
terms.art: A sticky, misty monsoon street with clothes hanging on a balcony that will not dry.

terms.meaning: Heatstroke is when the body gets dangerously hot and cannot cool itself down. It needs a doctor quickly.
terms.example: In a strong heatwave, people working in the sun can get heatstroke.
terms.art: A person resting in shade being given water and fanned, with a doctor's bag nearby.

terms.meaning: ORS means oral rehydration solution. It is clean water with the right amount of salt and sugar mixed in. It puts back water and salt the body has lost.
terms.example: When someone has loose motions, a doctor may say to sip ORS.
terms.art: A small ORS packet beside a steel tumbler of water and a spoon.

explanations.definition: Homeostasis is the way a living thing keeps its inside steady and just right, even when the outside keeps changing.
explanations.description: Your body needs many things to stay just right. It needs the right warmth, the right amount of water, the right amount of salt and the right amount of sugar in the blood. If any of these goes too high or too low for long, the body cannot work well. So the body keeps checking each one, and fixing it when it drifts. Keeping balance takes small corrections all the time. Riding a bicycle is similar: you stay upright by steering a little left, then a little right.
examples: On a hot day you sweat, and on a cold day you shiver. Both keep you near 37 degrees.
When you have lost water, you feel thirsty, and you drink.
When you have not eaten for a while, you feel hungry. Food brings your blood sugar back up.
explanations.art: A child riding a bicycle on a wobbly path, with little arrows showing tiny steering corrections left and right.
explanations.context: This card explains the main idea of the whole unit: homeostasis, the body keeping itself just right.

explanations.concept: The body's thermostat: notice, decide, act
explanations.definition: A feedback loop is a circle of three steps. A sensor notices a change. A control centre decides what to do. The body acts to undo the change.
explanations.description: Tiny sensors in your skin feel warmth. They send messages along nerves to your hypothalamus. That is a small part of your brain, about the size of an almond. It also feels the warmth of the blood flowing through it. It compares your warmth with the set point, the 'just right' number, which is about 37 degrees. If you are too warm, it tells your skin to sweat. If you are too cold, it tells your muscles to shiver. As you get back to just right, the sweating or shivering stops. Scientists call this negative feedback, because the action works against the change. An AC with a thermostat works the same way.
examples: An AC set to 26 degrees switches on when the room is warmer, and off when the room is cool enough.
A geyser heats water and switches off when the water is hot enough.
In your overhead water tank, a floating ball rises as the tank fills and shuts the tap off.
explanations.art: A loop of three arrows around a child: a skin sensor with a thermometer, a glowing almond-shaped spot in the brain, and a sweating forehead.
explanations.context: This card explains how your body keeps its warmth just right, using a loop of noticing, deciding and acting.

explanations.concept: Sweating cools you because the sweat dries
explanations.definition: Sweat cools you when it evaporates, which means when it dries into the air. Drying takes heat away from your skin.
explanations.description: Sweat itself is not cold. It comes out as warm as you are. The cooling happens when it dries. Water is made of tiny particles called molecules, always jiggling. The fastest ones fly off into the air first. They carry heat energy away with them. So the water left behind, and your skin under it, gets cooler. That is why a fan feels so good on a sweaty back. The moving air helps the sweat dry faster. Sweat that drips off onto the floor does not cool you much, because it did not dry on your skin. A grown-up working hard on a hot day can sweat more than a litre in an hour. Drinking water puts it back.
examples: A wet hand held in front of a fan feels colder than a dry hand.
A clay matka keeps water cool because a little water seeps out and dries on its outside.
After a bath, you feel chilly until you dry off.
explanations.art: A zoomed-in drop of sweat on skin, with a few fast little balls flying off it carrying red 'heat' sparks.
explanations.context: This card explains why sweating cools you down. Remember the tumbler test, where a wet cloth cooled one tumbler faster than a dry cloth cooled the other.

explanations.definition: When you are too cold, your body makes more heat and tries to keep the heat it has. Shivering makes heat. Goosebumps and curling up help to keep it.
explanations.description: Muscles make heat whenever they work. When you shiver, your muscles tighten and loosen very fast, by themselves. You do not move anywhere, but you make a lot of heat. Shivering can make a few times more heat than sitting still. At the same time, tiny muscles in your skin pull each hair upright. These are goosebumps. In a furry animal like a cat or a monkey, standing fur traps a warm layer of air. Our body hair is too thin to trap much, so goosebumps are a leftover from our furry relatives. Curling up into a ball also helps. It means less of your skin touches the cold air, so less heat escapes.
examples: Your teeth chatter when you come out of a cold swimming pool.
A cat fluffs up its fur on a cold winter morning.
Babies have a special brown fat that makes heat without shivering.
explanations.art: A shivering child in a towel beside a fluffed-up cat, both with tiny wavy heat lines.
explanations.context: This card explains what your body does when it is too cold.

explanations.concept: Red cheeks and white fingers: blood carries the heat
explanations.definition: Your blood carries heat around your body. Your body sends more blood near the skin to lose heat, and less blood near the skin to keep heat.
explanations.description: Blood flows through tubes called blood vessels. The blood is warm, because it passes through your busy insides. When you are hot, the tiny vessels near your skin open wider. More warm blood flows near the skin, and heat escapes into the air. That is why your face goes pink after running. When you are cold, those vessels squeeze narrow. Less blood goes to your skin, fingers and toes. Your middle stays warm, but your fingers turn pale and cold. The body is choosing to keep heat around your heart and brain, where it matters most.
examples: Your cheeks go red after a game of kho-kho.
Your fingers go white and stiff after holding an ice lolly for a long time.
An elephant flaps its huge ears. They are full of blood vessels, and the flapping cools the blood.
explanations.art: Two hands side by side: one pink with wide glowing blood tubes, one pale with thin tubes, and a small snowflake beside it.
explanations.context: This card explains why your skin changes colour when you are hot or cold.

explanations.definition: Your body keeps the amount of water inside you just right. Thirst tells you to drink more, and your kidneys decide how much water to let go as pee.
explanations.description: More than half of your body is water. Every day you lose some of it, in sweat, in pee and even in your breath. When your blood has too little water, it becomes a little too salty. Sensors in your hypothalamus notice this saltiness. They make you feel thirsty. They also send a chemical message to your kidneys, which says 'save water'. Then your pee becomes less and darker. When you have had plenty to drink, your pee is pale and you go to the toilet more often. Thirst is your body asking for water before things go wrong.
examples: On a hot day you drink more and pee less.
Pale yellow pee usually means you have had enough to drink. Dark yellow pee usually means drink more.
Breathe on a cold mirror. The mist is water leaving your body.
explanations.art: A water drop with a gauge on it: too little (dark pee jar, thirsty face), just right (pale jar, happy face), plenty (very pale jar, toilet).
explanations.context: This card explains why you feel thirsty, and how your body keeps the right amount of water inside.

explanations.concept: Why sticky monsoon days feel hotter
explanations.definition: Humidity is how much water is already in the air. When the air is very humid, sweat dries slowly, so it cools you less.
explanations.description: Remember, sweat cools you only when it dries. Air can hold only so much water. In Rajasthan in May, the air is very dry, and sweat dries almost as soon as it comes out. In Chennai or Mumbai during the monsoon, the air is already full of water. Your sweat sits on your skin and drips off. You feel sticky and hot, even at the same temperature. That is why weather reports sometimes give a 'feels like' temperature. It adds in the humidity.
examples: Wet clothes dry fast on a dry, windy day, and slowly on a damp monsoon day.
You feel sticky in a crowded, closed room.
A desert cooler works well in Delhi in May, but poorly in Kolkata in July.
explanations.art: Two scenes: a dry desert with sweat drops quickly vanishing into the air, and a misty monsoon street with sweat drops running down a sticky face.
explanations.context: This card explains why the same temperature can feel much hotter when the air is damp.

explanations.concept: How hot is too hot for a person?
explanations.description: If the air is very hot and also very humid, sweat can hardly dry, so it stops cooling you. Then your body cannot get rid of its heat, and it heats up. This is dangerous, and it is called heatstroke. Scientists measure this danger with a 'wet-bulb' temperature, which mixes heat and humidity into one number. They agree there is a limit. They do not agree exactly where it is, and it is different for babies, old people, sick people and people working hard.
examples: Heatwaves in India and Pakistan already come close to the danger limit on some days.
People working outside, like builders and farmers, are most at risk.
Shade, water, rest and wet cloths help the body keep up.

perspectives.explanation: They worked out a limit on paper. A wet-bulb temperature of 35 degrees, even for a healthy person resting in the shade with plenty of water, would be the edge of survival.

perspectives.who: Daniel Vecellio, Larry Kenney and others, 2022
perspectives.explanation: They tested young, healthy people in a hot, humid room. Their bodies could not keep steady at a lower number, about 31 degrees wet-bulb. So the real limit may be lower than the paper limit.
They found weather stations, including in Pakistan and around the Persian Gulf, where the 35 degree level had already been reached for an hour or two.

explanations.art: A thermometer with a humidity drop beside it, and a worker resting in shade drinking water.
explanations.context: This card is about a question scientists are still working on: how much heat and humidity a human body can survive.

explanations.description: Nobody knows for sure why mammals like us keep ourselves at about 37 degrees. Being warm costs a lot of food. A lizard, which does not keep itself warm, can eat far less than a mouse of the same size. So why pay so much? Scientists have ideas, but no final answer.
examples: Birds are even warmer than us, about 40 to 42 degrees.
A lizard warms up by lying on a hot rock in the sun.
A lizard is slow on a cold morning until the sun warms it. A mouse can run fast even on a cold night.

perspectives.explanation: Their idea is that 37 degrees is too hot for most fungi, the moulds and yeasts, to grow in us. It is also not so hot that we must eat all day. They worked out that about 36.7 degrees balances the two best.
They think being warm let early mammals stay quick and active at night and in the cold. The exact number might partly be an accident of history.

explanations.art: A lizard basking on a hot rock beside a mouse and a sparrow, each with a small thermometer.
explanations.context: This card is about a mystery: why our bodies keep about 37 degrees as just right.

explanations.concept: Does the body react, or does it predict?
explanations.description: The usual story is that the body waits for a change, then fixes it. But the body often acts before the change arrives. When you drink water, your thirst goes away in about a minute. That is long before the water has reached your blood. Your mouth and throat tell your brain 'water is coming'. In the same way, your body gets ready for food at the smell of dinner.
examples: Thirst goes away soon after you drink, before the water is used.
Your mouth waters when you smell parathas being cooked.
Many people's bodies start warming up just before they wake in the morning.

perspectives.explanation: The body has set points, and it corrects any drift away from them. This is homeostasis.
They said the brain mostly predicts what the body will need, and changes the set points to match. They called this allostasis.
They found thirst cells in the brains of mice that switch off within moments of drinking. The cells were predicting, before the blood changed.

explanations.art: A child drinking water, with a little arrow from the throat to the brain saying 'water coming!' while the water is still in the tummy.
explanations.context: This card is about a new way of looking at homeostasis: the body may predict, not only react.

explanations.definition: A living body uses energy, all the time, to stay different from its surroundings. Without that energy, it would slowly drift to the same warmth as the room.
explanations.description: Leave a cup of hot chai on the table. It cools down until it is the same warmth as the room. That is what non-living things do. A hot thing always gives heat to a colder thing, until they are equal. You do not drift like the chai. That is because your cells are always using food to make heat. Even sitting still, a grown-up gives off about as much heat as an old-fashioned 100 watt bulb. The physicist Erwin Schrödinger wrote about this in 1944, in a small book called What Is Life? He said living things stay ordered by taking in energy and giving out heat. So keeping your warmth steady needs food every day.
examples: A cup of hot chai always cools to the room's warmth.
A crowded room gets warm from all the people's body heat.
Food is your fuel. A child eats every day partly to keep warm.
explanations.art: A cooling cup of chai with fading steam, beside a child glowing a steady warm orange from inside.
explanations.context: This card is about why keeping balance needs food and energy, and is not free.

explanations.definition: Homeostasis is not only for humans. Every living thing, even one tiny cell, keeps its inside different from its outside, and just right.
explanations.description: Each of your cells has tiny pumps in its skin. They push one kind of salt out and pull another kind in, all day long. A big share of the energy you use at rest goes into these pumps. Bacteria do it too. Animals have many clever ways to stay just right. Dogs have sweat glands only on their paw pads, so they pant to cool down. Camels let their warmth go up by about 6 degrees during a hot day, to save water from sweating. Storks and some vultures wee on their own legs to cool off. Honeybees keep the middle of their hive at about 35 degrees. They fan with their wings, and spread water drops to cool it. Some sacred lotus flowers even keep themselves warm, at about 30 to 35 degrees, on cool nights.
examples: A dog pants with its tongue out on a hot afternoon.
A camel crosses the desert with little water.
A lotus flower in a pond can be warmer than the air around it.
explanations.art: A row of balance-keepers: a panting dog, a camel, a stork, a beehive with fanning bees, and a pink lotus with a tiny thermometer.
explanations.context: This card shows that every living thing, from a cell to a beehive, keeps its own balance.

explanations.concept: Does the Earth keep its own balance?
explanations.description: The Earth has stayed warm enough for liquid water, and for life, for more than three billion years. That is surprising, because the Sun was dimmer long ago. Some scientists think the Earth has its own slow thermostat. Others think part of the reason is luck.
examples: Rain slowly washes carbon dioxide out of the air into rocks. This happens faster when the Earth is warm, so it cools the Earth down.
Tiny sea plants and trees change the air, and so change the weather.
Today, people are adding carbon dioxide faster than any slow thermostat can fix.

perspectives.explanation: Their Gaia idea says living things and the Earth together act like one self-regulating system that keeps conditions good for life.

perspectives.who: James Walker, Paul Hays and James Kasting, 1981
perspectives.explanation: They described a slow rock thermostat that works even without life. Warmth speeds up rain and rock weathering, which pulls carbon dioxide out of the air. It takes hundreds of thousands of years.
They agree there are balancing loops, but they say the Earth is not a body with a set point. Some loops even push it further away from balance, like melting ice making the Earth darker and warmer.

explanations.art: The Earth drawn with a small dial on it, arrows of rain, rocks, forests and ocean plankton around it in a loop.
explanations.context: This card goes out to the whole planet: does the Earth keep itself just right, like a body?

explanations.description: In 1868, a German doctor called Carl Wunderlich said normal body temperature is 37 degrees. He used about a million readings from about 25,000 people. But today, many studies find healthy people are a little cooler, closer to 36.6 degrees. Each person also has their own normal. You are cooler in the early morning and warmer in the late afternoon.
examples: Your temperature under your arm is a little lower than in your mouth.
You are slightly warmer after running, and cooler when you have just woken up.
Old people are often a little cooler than children.

perspectives.who: Myroslava Protsiv, Julie Parsonnet and others, 2020
perspectives.explanation: They studied old army records and modern records in the USA. People's temperatures have dropped by about half a degree in 150 years. They think less illness and comfortable homes may be the reason.
They say the old thermometers and methods were different, so some of the change may be in the measuring, not in the bodies.

explanations.art: An old doctor in a Victorian coat with a long thermometer, next to a modern digital thermometer reading 36.6.
explanations.context: This card is about whether 37 degrees is really 'normal' for everyone.

agreed.text: The inside of a healthy human body stays at about 37 degrees, whatever the weather.
agreed.evidence: Doctors have measured millions of people in hot and cold countries. Their inside temperature stays within about one degree of 37, unless they are ill.

agreed.text: Sweat cools the body when it dries on the skin.
agreed.evidence: A wet thing in moving air cools faster than a dry one. You can measure this with two tumblers and a thermometer. In very humid air, where sweat cannot dry, people get hotter.
Scientists measure how much oxygen people use. A shivering person can use several times more, because their muscles are working hard and making heat.

agreed.text: A part of the brain called the hypothalamus controls warmth, thirst and hunger.
agreed.evidence: In animal experiments, warming or cooling a tiny spot in this part of the brain makes the animal sweat, pant or shiver, even when the rest of its body is normal.

agreed.text: Thirst and the kidneys keep the body's water balanced.
agreed.evidence: When people drink less, their pee becomes darker and smaller in amount. When they drink more, their pee becomes paler and larger in amount. Blood tests show the saltiness of the blood stays nearly the same.

agreed.text: Losing too much water and salt can be dangerous, and ORS can save lives.
agreed.evidence: In 1971, in refugee camps near the Bangladesh border, Dr Dilip Mahalanabis and his team gave ORS to people with cholera when there was not enough drip fluid. Far fewer people died than usual. Since then ORS has saved many millions of lives.

challenging.claim: Normal body temperature is exactly 37.0 degrees for everyone.
challenging.who: Many people, and many old books, following Carl Wunderlich's work in 1868.
challenging.for: Wunderlich measured many thousands of people, and the average was close to 37.
challenging.against: Each person has their own normal. It changes through the day. Many modern studies find an average a little below 37, closer to 36.6. So 37 is a rough guide, not an exact rule.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that 37 degrees is exactly normal for all people.

challenging.claim: If you sweat a lot, you must be unfit or dirty.
challenging.who: A common idea, and many advertisements.
challenging.for: Sweat can smell when bacteria on the skin feed on it.
challenging.against: Sweating is your body working well. Fit people often start to sweat sooner, because their bodies have learned to cool down quickly. Sweat itself has almost no smell.
challenging.context: This card is about whether sweating is a bad thing.

challenging.claim: Humans became such great sweaters so they could hunt by running animals down in the heat.
challenging.for: Humans have millions of sweat glands and little fur. We can run long distances in the heat better than most animals. A few groups of hunters have done this kind of running hunt.
challenging.against: Other scientists say running hunts were rare. Sweating may have helped early humans walk and work in hot open land, without any hunting.
challenging.context: This card is about why humans sweat so much more than most animals.

challenging.claim: You must drink exactly 8 glasses of water every day.
challenging.who: A popular rule you may hear at school or on posters.
challenging.for: Many people do need about that much, especially in a hot country like India.
challenging.against: In 2002, a scientist called Heinz Valtin looked for proof of this exact rule and did not find it. How much you need depends on your size, the weather, how active you are, and how much water is in your food. Thirst and pee colour are good guides for a healthy child.
challenging.context: This card is about the rule that everyone needs 8 glasses of water a day.

challenging.claim: The Earth is like one living body that keeps itself just right.
challenging.who: James Lovelock and Lynn Margulis, the Gaia idea, 1970s.
challenging.for: The Earth has stayed good for life for billions of years, even as the Sun got brighter. Living things do change the air and the weather.
challenging.against: A body has a set point that it defends. The Earth does not seem to have one. Some Earth changes push it further from balance, not back towards it.
challenging.context: This card is about whether the whole Earth keeps its balance, the way a body does.

challenging.claim: Health is a balance of three doshas, vata, pitta and kapha.
challenging.who: Ayurveda, India's old system of medicine, still used by many families.
challenging.for: Like homeostasis, it says health is balance, and it pays close attention to heat, cold, food, water and sleep.
challenging.against: Scientists have not found doshas as things that can be measured in the body. Science measures temperature, water, salt and sugar instead. Treatments must be tested carefully either way.
challenging.context: This card is about an old Indian idea of health as balance, and how it compares with homeostasis.

how_we_found_out.story: In 1918, the American scientist Walter Cannon, who later named homeostasis, said that thirst was simply the feeling of a dry mouth. When the body is low on water, he said, it makes less spit, the mouth dries, and so we want to drink. It sounded sensible, but other experiments did not fit. In the 1930s, scientists studied dogs whose swallowed water ran out through a small tube in the neck, so it never reached the stomach. Their mouths were wet, yet they drank, stopped for a short while, and then drank again and again. In 1953, the Swedish scientist Bengt Andersson put a tiny drop of very salty water into the hypothalamus of some goats. The goats' mouths were not dry, and their bodies were not short of water. Within a minute or two they began to drink, and they drank several litres. So thirst starts in the brain, when it senses that the blood has become too salty. A wet mouth stops thirst only for a short time.
how_we_found_out.who: Walter Cannon (the dry mouth idea), and the scientists who tested it, including Bengt Andersson
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That thirst is only the feeling of a dry mouth.

big_questions.q: Sweat comes out as warm as you are. So how can it cool you down?
big_questions.hint: Think about wet clothes drying on a line. Where does the water go, and what does it take with it?

big_questions.q: Why do you shiver even when you don't want to?
big_questions.hint: Who decides to shiver? Is it you, or a part of you that works without asking?

big_questions.q: If your body is always changing water, heat and atoms, are you the same 'you' as last year?
big_questions.hint: Think of a river. The water is always new, but we still call it the same river.

big_questions.q: Why do you feel thirsty as a feeling, instead of your body just quietly fixing itself?
big_questions.hint: What would happen if your body needed water, but you never felt like drinking?

big_questions.q: Is 'just right' the same for everyone?
big_questions.hint: Is your mother's comfortable room warmth the same as yours? Is your normal temperature the same as a friend's?

big_questions.q: In a heatwave, who can cool down easily, and who cannot?
big_questions.hint: Think about a person with an AC in an office, and a person carrying bricks on a building site.

big_questions.q: A beehive keeps its middle at about 35 degrees, but no single bee is in charge. How can a hive keep balance with no boss?
big_questions.hint: Each bee fans its wings or fetches water when the place where it stands gets too warm.

big_questions.q: Does the Earth have a thermostat?
big_questions.hint: Think of what rain, forests and oceans do to the air.

big_questions.q: When you have a fever, your body moves its 'just right' number up. Why might a body want to be hotter when it is ill?
big_questions.hint: Many germs grow more slowly when it is warmer.

story.title: The Pot That Sweats
story.note: Imagined. The village, Ruksana, Imran and their mother are made up. It is true that a clay matka cools water because water seeps through and dries on its outside, and that heatwaves in western Rajasthan can pass 45 degrees.
text: I am a pot. I am made of the brown earth of the riverbank, shaped on a wheel and baked in a fire. I sit in the corner of a small house at the edge of the desert, near Barmer, on a little stand of bricks. People call me the matka. I have no eyes, no ears and no heart. But I have a skin full of tiny holes, so small that you cannot see them. Through those holes, I feel everything.

Every morning, Ruksana fills me. She is ten, and she walks to the hand pump before the sun is up. She pours the water in carefully, so that it does not slop. Then she puts a steel plate on my head and a tumbler on the plate. All day long, the family comes to me. They lift the plate, dip the tumbler, and drink.

That May was the hottest May anybody could remember. The air shook above the sand. The goats lay flat in the thin shade of the khejri tree and would not get up. At noon the radio said forty-seven degrees, and then it said nothing at all, because the electricity went off. The fan in the ceiling slowed down, turned once more, and stopped.

Imran, Ruksana's little brother, was four. He did not like the heat. He did not like anything that day. He cried, and kicked his sheet off the charpai, and cried again. His cheeks were red as chillies. His hair stuck to his forehead in wet curls. Their mother had gone to the next village to help her sister, and she would not be back until the evening.
"Drink," said Ruksana. She dipped the tumbler into me and held it to his mouth. He drank a little, made a face, and pushed it away. "It's not cold," he said. "It's never cold. I want cold."

He was wrong, of course. My water is always cooler than the air. Nobody in that house ever asked why. They thought I was simply a cold sort of thing, the way a stone is hard. But I am not cold at all. I am clay, baked in a fire. Left empty in the sun, I would be as hot as a roof.

Here is my secret. A little of the water inside me creeps out through my tiny holes. It spreads over my outside in a thin, damp skin. And then the dry desert air drinks it. Each tiny bit of water that flies away takes a little heat with it. So I am always giving a little away, and that is why the rest stays cool. When the air is damp, in the monsoon, I do not work so well. But in May, with the hot dry wind blowing, I work better than ever.

Ruksana sat on the floor beside her brother and wiped her own face with her dupatta. She was hot too. She leaned back against me. And for the first time, she noticed. My side was cool. Not wet, not dripping, just cool and a little damp, like a forehead in the evening. She turned and put both palms flat on me. Then she put her cheek against me, and closed her eyes.
"Ammi says the matka sweats," she said, half to herself. "That's why it stays cool."

She sat up straight. She looked at her little brother, red and cross and dry-eyed now, too tired even to cry. His skin had been wet an hour ago. Now it looked dry and hot, and that frightened her more than the crying.

Ruksana took the thin cotton cloth from the shelf, the one Ammi used for rotis. She dipped it into me, deep, and wrung it out until it was only damp. She laid it over Imran's arms and his legs and the back of his neck. Then she picked up the hand fan made of palm leaves and began to fan him. Slowly, steadily, the way the dry wind fans me.
"I'm making you into a matka," she said.

He almost laughed. She kept fanning. Each time the cloth began to dry, she dipped it again. She found the ORS packet that Ammi kept in the tin by the door. She mixed it into a tumbler of my water, exactly as the picture on the packet showed, and gave it to him in small sips. She did not make him gulp it. A sip, then fanning. A sip, then fanning.

The shadow of the khejri tree crept across the yard. Imran's cheeks went from chilli red to pink. His breathing slowed. Then, at last, small beads of sweat came back onto his forehead, and he fell asleep. Ruksana kept fanning, very gently, until her arm ached.

When their mother came home in the cool of the evening, she found the two of them asleep on the floor beside me. The damp cloth was still over Imran's legs. The palm fan was still in Ruksana's hand. Ammi put the back of her fingers on her son's forehead, then on her daughter's. She went to the neighbour's house to fetch the nurse, just to be safe. Then she sat down beside me, and dipped the tumbler, and drank for a long time.

People think that keeping cool means holding on to cold. It does not. I have never held on to anything. I stay cool because I let a little go, all the time, into the hot air. Ruksana understood that, that day, with her cheek against my side. I think she understood something else too, though I am only a pot, and I may be wrong. Her brother's body had been doing the same thing all along. It had only needed someone to help it.
story.epiphany: For the parent: the matka is cool not because it is a cold thing, but because water seeps out and evaporates from its surface, carrying heat away. Ruksana's turn is realising that sweat works the same way, and that her brother's body had become too hot and dry to cool itself. A damp cloth and fanning do what sweat does, and ORS puts back water and salt. In real life, a hot, dry, floppy child in a heatwave needs a doctor or nurse quickly.
ask: Why was the water in the matka cooler than the air, even though the matka is made of baked clay?
What did Ruksana notice when she put her cheek against the matka?
Why did Ruksana dip the cloth in water and fan her brother? What was she copying?
Why do you think dry, hot skin frightened Ruksana more than the crying?
The pot says it stays cool 'because it lets a little go'. What do you think it means?

games.title: Keep It Just Right
games.players: 2 to 4 players, or one child playing against the app
games.context: Keep It Just Right is a card game about homeostasis. Each player has a body warmth dial. Event cards push it hot or cold, and body action cards bring it back to just right.

printables.title: One warmth dial for each player
items: A row of 9 boxes, numbered 1 to 9

printables.title: 20 event cards (red pushes up, blue pushes down)
items: Wore a sweater indoors in May: +2
Sat in a closed car in the sun: +3
Got a fever: +2 (and see a doctor in real life)
Wind blew on a wet back: -2
Drank cold water from a matka: -1
Sat still in a cold room: -1

printables.title: 16 body action cards
items: Cheeks go red, blood to the skin: -1
Cheeks go red, blood to the skin: -1
Drink water: take a used Sweat card back into your hand
Drink water: take a used Sweat card back into your hand

printables.title: One counter for each player's dial, and 15 'just right' stars

rules: Each player puts a counter on box 5 of their dial, the green JUST RIGHT box.
Shuffle the red and blue event cards into one pile. Deal 4 body action cards to each player.
On your turn, turn over the top event card and move your counter up or down by that number.
Then you may play one body action card from your hand to move back towards 5. Say what your body is doing, out loud.
If your counter is on 5 at the end of your turn, you win a star.
At the end of every turn, pick up one new body action card. When that pile runs out, shuffle the played body cards to make a new pile.
If your counter reaches 1 or 9, you have gone too far. Miss a turn while you rest and drink water, then move back to 3 or 7.
After 15 event cards, the player with the most stars wins.

flow.do: 1. Give each player a dial and a counter on box 5. 2. Shuffle the event cards. 3. Deal 4 body action cards to each player.
flow.say: Your body likes to stay at just right. That is box 5. The weather and what you do will push you hot or cold. Your job is to bring yourself back, like your real body does.
flow.kid: Put your counter on box 5. That is just right. Events will push you hot or cold. Use your body cards to come back to 5.
flow.context: This is the first step of Keep It Just Right, a card game about how your body keeps its warmth steady. Here you set up the game.

flow.do: Play one practice round together. Turn over 'Played cricket at noon: +2'. Move to 7.
flow.say: We played cricket at noon, so we go up 2, to box 7. That is warm. What could your body do to come back to 5?
flow.kid: Practice card: played cricket at noon, plus 2. You are on 7 now. Which body card brings you back?

ask.q: Why does sweating bring you down?
good: When sweat dries, it takes heat away.
The fastest water molecules fly off and carry heat.

check.q: You are on 7, too warm. Which body card brings you back to 5?
check.why: Sweat brings you down 2, from 7 to 5. When sweat dries on your skin, it carries heat away. Shiver and goosebumps would push you even hotter, because they make or keep heat. Picking them is a good game moment to ask: which actions warm us, and which cool us?

flow.context: This is a practice round of Keep It Just Right, the body warmth card game.

flow.do: Take turns. Each player turns over an event card, moves, then plays one body card and says what their body is doing.
flow.say: When you play a body card, tell us what your body is really doing. For example: 'My sweat is drying and taking heat away.'
flow.kid: Your turn. Turn over an event card. Move your counter. Play a body card. Say what your body is doing.
flow.parent: Listen for real reasons. Good ones: 'my blood vessels open so heat escapes', 'my muscles shake to make heat', 'I curl up so less skin touches the cold'. The 'Drink water' card matters: without water, you cannot keep sweating. Notice the humid monsoon card pushes you up because sweat dries slowly.
flow.context: This is the main part of Keep It Just Right. Players keep their body warmth dial at just right.

flow.do: When someone reaches 1 or 9, stop the game for a moment and talk about it.
flow.say: You reached the edge! In real life, that is when the body cannot fix it alone. What would a grown-up do to help?
flow.kid: You reached the edge. Your body needs help now. What can a grown-up do?

ask.q: What helps a person who is far too hot?
good: Shade, water and a wet cloth.
Call a doctor if they are confused or floppy.

ask.q: What helps a person who is far too cold?
good: A blanket, a warm room and a warm drink.

flow.context: This is a step in Keep It Just Right. It is about what happens when the body cannot keep balance alone.

flow.do: Count the stars. Ask each player which body card helped them most.
flow.say: Who has the most stars? Which body card did you use most? When did you need to drink water?
flow.kid: Count your stars. Which body card helped you most?
flow.think: Your real body plays this game all day and all night. Who is playing it while you sleep?
flow.context: This is the last step of Keep It Just Right, the body warmth card game.

games.title: Brain Says
games.players: 2 or more players, best with a grown-up calling
games.context: Brain Says is a quick moving game. The grown-up is the brain. They call out what is happening, and the players act out what the body does to stay just right.
rules: One person is the Brain and holds the caller cards.
The Brain reads a card. The players act out what the body does. For example, wipe sweat for 'Hot sun!' and shiver for 'Cold wind!'.
For 'Just right!', everyone stands still and smiles.
If a player does a cooling action for a cold card, or a warming action for a hot card, they explain what went wrong and then carry on.
Swap who is the Brain after 6 cards.

flow.do: Stand in a clear space. Show the players the actions: wipe sweat and fan for hot, shiver and hug yourself for cold, pretend to drink for thirsty.
flow.say: I am your brain. I will tell you what is happening. You show me what your body does to stay just right.
flow.kid: The grown-up is the brain. Listen to the call. Show what your body does.
flow.context: This is the first step of Brain Says, an acting game about how the body keeps balance.

flow.do: Read the caller cards one at a time, fast. After each, ask one player why.
flow.say: Hot sun! Cold wind! Very thirsty! Now tell me, why did you shiver when I said cold wind?
flow.kid: Listen and act fast. Hot? Cold? Thirsty? Then say why you did it.

check.q: The Brain says 'Snow on the mountain!' What does your body do?
check.why: In the cold, your muscles shiver to make heat, and goosebumps try to trap warmth. Sweating and red cheeks are for losing heat, which you do when you are too hot. Mixing them up is common, so try acting out one hot card and one cold card again.

flow.context: This is the main part of Brain Says, the acting game about keeping warm or cool.

flow.do: End with the 'Just right!' card. Ask the players to stand still, breathe slowly and feel their warmth.
flow.say: Just right! Stand still. Feel how warm your hands are. Your body has stopped sweating and shivering, because it is just right.
flow.kid: Just right! Stand still. Breathe slowly. Feel your warm hands.
flow.think: When you are just right, is your body doing nothing? Or is it still checking?
flow.context: This is the last step of Brain Says. It ends with being just right.
