items.p: What does homeostasis mean?
opts: Keeping the inside of the body steady and just right
items.why: Homeostasis is the body keeping things like warmth and water just right. Picking 'growing' mixes it up with change. Homeostasis is about staying the same inside while the outside changes.

items.p: About how warm is the inside of a healthy person?
opts: It changes with the weather, from 10 to 45 degrees
items.why: A healthy body stays near 37 degrees. Picking 'it changes with the weather' is a common idea, because our skin feels hot or cold. But the inside stays steady. That is the whole point of homeostasis.

items.p: When you are hot, your skin makes salty water called ____.
items.why: Sweat comes from millions of tiny sweat glands in your skin.

items.p: How does sweat cool you down?
opts: It dries into the air and carries heat away
Sweat is cold when it comes out
items.why: When sweat evaporates, the fastest water molecules fly off and take heat with them. Picking 'sweat is cold' is very common. But sweat comes out as warm as you are. The cooling comes from drying.
items.art: A sweaty forehead with little wavy lines rising off it.

items.p: What do your muscles do when you are very cold?
items.why: Shivering is fast shaking of the muscles, and working muscles make heat. Picking 'sweat' mixes up the cooling trick with the warming trick.

items.p: Sort these. Does the body do this to COOL DOWN or to KEEP WARM?
items.why: Sweating, red skin and panting all help heat escape. Shivering makes heat. Goosebumps and pale fingers help keep the heat in. Pale fingers might look like 'cold', but the body is saving heat for its middle.

items.p: Feeling thirsty is your body telling you it needs water.
items.why: True. When you have lost water, your blood gets a little too salty. Your brain notices and makes you feel thirsty.

items.p: Which part of your body decides when to sweat or shiver?
opts: A small part of your brain called the hypothalamus
items.why: The hypothalamus is about the size of an almond, deep in your brain. It compares your warmth with 'just right' and decides. Your skin and muscles only carry out the order.

items.p: Match each thing to what it does.
items.why: A feedback loop has something that notices, something that decides and something that acts.

items.p: Remember the sweaty tumbler test? One tumbler of warm water had a wet cloth, one had a dry cloth, both in front of a fan. Which cooled more?
items.why: Water drying from the wet cloth carried heat away. Picking 'both the same' often means thinking the fan does all the work. The fan helps, but it mostly works by drying the wet cloth.

items.p: Why do your cheeks go red after running?
opts: More warm blood flows near the skin to let heat out
items.why: When you are hot, the blood vessels near your skin open wider. More warm blood passes near the air, and heat escapes. Cheeks can also go red when you feel shy, but after running it is about cooling.

items.p: Put the sweating loop in order.
items: The hypothalamus decides to cool you
The sweat dries and you cool down
items.why: Notice, decide, act, and then check again. When you are just right, the loop switches the sweating off.

items.p: Which of these is a good sign that you have drunk enough water?
items.why: Pale yellow pee usually means your kidneys have plenty of water to let go. Dark pee, dizziness and a dry mouth can all mean you need to drink.

items.p: Why does a fan feel good when you are sweaty? Use the word 'dry' in your answer.
items.a: The moving air helps my sweat dry faster. When sweat dries, it carries heat away from my skin, so I cool down.
items.why: Sweat cools you by drying, and moving air helps it dry.

items.p: Draw yourself on a hot day and on a cold day. Label two things your body does in each.
items.a: Hot: sweat, red cheeks. Cold: shivering, goosebumps or pale fingers.
items.why: The body has tricks for cooling and tricks for warming. Each one helps keep you near 37 degrees.
items.art: Two empty outlines of a child, one under a sun and one under a snowflake.

items.p: A clay matka keeps water cool. Why?
opts: Water seeps out and dries on its outside, carrying heat away
items.why: The matka 'sweats'. Water creeps through tiny holes and dries on the outside. Picking 'clay is always cold' is common. But a dry clay pot left in the sun gets very hot.

items.p: A sweaty child sits in a closed, humid room. Why do they still feel hot?
opts: The damp air makes sweat dry slowly, so it cools them less
Humid air has more heat in it than any other air
items.why: Sweat cools only when it dries. In humid air, it dries slowly and drips off instead. Picking 'sweat does not work indoors' misses that it is the dampness of the air, not the room, that matters.

items.p: Remember the My Steady Inside test, where you took your temperature under your arm before and after running? Your face felt very hot after running, but your temperature only went up a tiny bit. Why?
opts: Your body got rid of the extra heat by sweating and sending blood to the skin
Your face is not part of your body
items.why: Running made heat, but homeostasis got rid of it fast. Your skin felt hot because warm blood was flowing there to lose heat.

items.p: The 'just right' number the body tries to stay at is called the ____ point.
items.why: The set point is like the number on an AC remote.

items.p: A camel in the desert lets its body warm up by about 6 degrees during the day, then cools at night. Why might this help it?
opts: It sweats less, so it saves water
It makes the camel run faster
items.why: If the camel kept itself at one exact warmth, it would have to sweat a lot in the hot day. By letting its warmth rise, it saves water. It cools off at night for free.

items.p: Why do dogs pant on a hot day?
opts: Water dries from their tongue and mouth, carrying heat away
items.why: Dogs have sweat glands only on their paw pads. Panting moves air over their wet tongue, so water dries and cools them. It is the same trick as sweating.

items.p: Sweat that drips off onto the floor cools you just as well as sweat that dries on your skin.
items.why: False. Sweat cools you when it dries on your skin, because drying takes heat from you. Sweat that drips off takes away very little heat.

items.p: You drink a glass of water when you are thirsty. Your thirst goes away in about a minute, long before the water reaches your blood. What does this show?
opts: The body predicts, using messages from the mouth and throat
Water goes straight into the brain
items.why: In mice, scientists found that brain cells for thirst switch off soon after drinking. Your body predicts that water is coming. This is part of a debate about whether the body mostly reacts or mostly predicts.

items.p: Match each animal or plant to its balance trick.
pairs: flaps big ears full of blood
fan their wings to cool the hive
fluffs up its fur to trap warm air
wees on its legs to cool off
items.why: Each living thing has its own ways to keep just right. Many of them use drying water or moving blood, like we do.

items.p: Why are your fingers and toes often the first to feel cold?
opts: The body sends less blood there in the cold, to keep the middle warm
They are furthest from the sun
They are made of bone only
items.why: In the cold, blood vessels near the skin and in the fingers squeeze narrow. The body is choosing to keep heat near the heart and brain.

items.p: A cup of hot chai cools to the warmth of the room. Why doesn't your body cool to the warmth of the room too?
items.a: My body keeps burning food in my cells to make heat. My brain keeps checking and fixing my warmth. The chai has nothing inside to make heat.
items.why: Staying steady costs energy. Living things use food to keep themselves different from their surroundings.

items.p: Which machine at home works most like your body's warmth loop?
opts: A ceiling fan with no switch
items.why: An AC notices the room's warmth, compares it with the set number, and switches cooling on or off. That is a feedback loop, like your hypothalamus and sweat.

items.p: Put the thirst loop in order.
items: Your blood gets a little too salty
The saltiness goes back to just right
items.why: Again: change, notice, decide, act, and back to just right.

items.p: Babies have something special to keep warm without shivering. What is it?
opts: Sweat glands that make warm sweat
items.why: Babies have patches of brown fat, especially around the neck and shoulders. It burns food to make heat directly. Adults have a little brown fat too.

items.p: Draw a feedback loop for being too cold. Use three arrows: notice, decide, act.
items.a: Skin sensors notice the cold. The hypothalamus decides. Muscles shiver and skin makes goosebumps. Then the body checks again.
items.why: Every feedback loop has the same shape, whether it is cooling or warming.
items.art: Three empty circles joined by arrows in a loop.

items.p: Why is 37 degrees our 'just right'?
opts: Nobody knows for sure. One idea is that it is too warm for most fungi to grow in us
Because a doctor chose it in 1868
items.why: It is still an open question. The fungi idea is from Aviv Bergman and Arturo Casadevall, 2010. A doctor only measured it. He did not choose it. Water boils at 100 degrees, not 37.

items.p: Remember the matka test, where a clay pot and a steel pot stood side by side with the same water? On which day would the matka cool its water best?
opts: A hot, dry, breezy day in May
A day when the matka is painted with oil paint
A day with no water inside
items.why: Drying water cools the matka. Dry, moving air dries it fastest. Humid, still air dries it slowly. Oil paint would block the tiny holes, so no water could reach the outside.

items.p: In a heatwave, why is it more dangerous for a builder carrying bricks than for a person sitting under a fan? Give two reasons.
items.a: The builder's muscles make much more heat while working. The builder is also in the sun, and may not have time to rest, drink or cool off. The person under the fan makes less heat, and the fan helps their sweat dry.
items.why: Heat danger depends on how much heat you make, how much you get from outside, and how well your sweat can dry. It is also a question of fairness: who gets shade, water and rest.

items.p: Some scientists say the body mostly predicts what it will need, not only reacts. Which is an example of predicting?
opts: Your mouth waters when you smell food cooking
You shiver after you are already cold
You sweat after you are already hot
You pull your hand from a hot pan after it hurts
items.why: A watering mouth gets ready for food before it arrives. The other three happen after the change. This idea is called allostasis, and scientists still argue how important it is.

items.p: In the sweaty tumbler test, the wet cloth tumbler went from 40 to 31 degrees. The dry cloth tumbler went from 40 to 37 degrees. The wet one dropped ____ degrees and the dry one dropped ____ degrees.
items.why: 40 take away 31 is 9. 40 take away 37 is 3. The wet one cooled 3 times as much.

items.p: A person who is very hot has stopped sweating and has hot, dry skin. They are confused. What should happen?
opts: Get them into shade, cool them with water, and call a doctor straight away
Tell them to run to cool down
items.why: Hot, dry skin and confusion can be signs of heatstroke. The body's cooling has stopped working. This needs a doctor fast. Shade and wet cloths help while you wait.

items.p: Scientists all agree that the whole Earth keeps itself just right, exactly like a body.
items.why: False. James Lovelock and Lynn Margulis's Gaia idea says something like this, but many scientists disagree. The Earth has balancing loops, but no fixed set point like a body.

items.p: Why does your body need food even when you are sitting still?
opts: To keep making heat and running the pumps in every cell
It doesn't need any food when still
items.why: Even at rest you give off about as much heat as an old 100 watt bulb. Every cell also pumps salt to keep its inside just right. All of this needs energy from food.

items.p: Dr Dilip Mahalanabis used ORS in refugee camps in 1971. Why does putting back salt as well as water help a person who has lost a lot of fluid?
items.a: The body loses salt as well as water. Blood needs the right saltiness. ORS puts back both, and the sugar in it helps the gut take up the salt and water.
items.why: Homeostasis keeps both water and salt just right. Losing one without the other upsets the balance.

items.p: Studies suggest people's normal temperature is a little lower today than 150 years ago. What is one possible reason scientists give?
opts: Fewer long-lasting illnesses and more comfortable homes
items.why: Myroslava Protsiv, Julie Parsonnet and others suggested less illness and comfortable homes. Others think old measuring methods were different. It is still debated.

items.p: Put these from the warmest normal body to the coolest: a sparrow, a human, a lizard on a cold morning.
items.why: Birds keep themselves at about 40 to 42 degrees. Humans are about 37. A lizard does not make much of its own heat, so on a cold morning it is as cold as the air until it basks.

items.p: Why can't goosebumps keep us warm the way fur keeps a cat warm?
opts: Our body hair is too thin and short to trap a layer of air
We have no muscles in our skin
Goosebumps make us hotter than cats
items.why: Goosebumps pull our hairs up, just like a cat's. But our hairs are too thin to trap a blanket of still air. So goosebumps are a leftover from our furry relatives.

items.p: Draw the Earth's slow rock thermostat as a loop: Earth gets warmer, more rain and weathering, less carbon dioxide in the air, Earth cools.
items.a: A loop of four arrows: warmer Earth, more rain washing rocks, less carbon dioxide, cooler Earth, back to the start.
items.why: This loop works over hundreds of thousands of years. It cannot fix fast changes, like the carbon dioxide people are adding today.
items.art: A blank circle with four empty boxes around it.

items.p: A lotus flower can keep itself at about 30 to 35 degrees on a cool night. What does this tell us?
opts: Some plants can do a kind of warmth homeostasis too
items.why: Scientists measured sacred lotus flowers in 1996 and found they keep themselves warm. Balance-keeping is not only for animals.

items.p: The matka in the story says: 'I stay cool because I let a little go.' How is your body like that?
items.a: My body lets a little water out as sweat. When the sweat dries, it takes heat from my skin. So, like the matka, I cool down by losing a little water.
items.why: Sweat cools you the same way the matka cools its water: water evaporates from the outside and carries heat away.

items.p: Which of these is NOT a feedback loop that keeps something steady?
opts: A ball rolling down a hill
An overhead water tank float that shuts the tap when full
A geyser that switches off when the water is hot
items.why: A rolling ball just keeps going. Nothing notices and corrects it. The other three all notice a change and act to undo it.

experiments.title: The Sweaty Tumbler Test
experiments.context: This is the sweaty tumbler test. You wrap two tumblers of warm water, one in a wet cloth and one in a dry cloth, and put them in front of a fan. Then you measure which one cools down faster.
experiments.question: Does a wet cloth, like sweat on skin, cool something down faster than a dry cloth?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which tumbler will be cooler after 20 minutes: the one in the wet cloth or the one in the dry cloth? Or will they be the same? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, keep everything the same except the wet cloth. Use two tumblers that are the same. Pour the same amount of the same warm water in each. Use the same kind of cloth. Put both the same distance from the fan.

materials.item: two steel tumblers that are the same
two cotton hankies or cloths that are the same
warm water, about as warm as a bath: mix hot water from the kettle with tap water
a thermometer, like a kitchen probe thermometer
a table fan or ceiling fan
a clock, a pencil and the results table

experiments.safety: A grown-up pours the warm water. It should feel comfortable to touch, like bath water, not hot. Keep fingers and the cloth away from the fan blades.

schedule.what: Guess. Wrap the tumblers. Measure every 5 minutes for 20 minutes. Fill in the table. Say what you found.

experiments.record: Fill in the table every 5 minutes. Then work out how many degrees each tumbler dropped. Draw one bar for each tumbler to show the drop.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: how many degrees each tumbler cooled in 20 minutes
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different.

setup.art: Two identical steel tumblers of warm water on a table, a grown-up's hand pouring the water.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up pours the same warm water into two tumblers.

setup.art: One tumbler wrapped in a dripping-damp cotton hanky and one in a dry hanky, both tied with a rubber band.
setup.caption: 2. Wrap one in a wet cloth and one in a dry cloth.

setup.art: Both wrapped tumblers side by side in front of a table fan, a thermometer probe in one, a clock behind.
setup.caption: 3. Put both in front of the fan. Measure each one every 5 minutes.

flow.do: 1. Show the two tumblers and the two cloths. 2. Ask your child to guess which will cool faster after 20 minutes.
flow.say: Your skin gets wet with sweat when you are hot. Does being wet really help you cool down? Let's test it with two tumblers. Which one will be cooler after 20 minutes, the wet one or the dry one?
flow.kid: You will test two tumblers of warm water. One wears a wet cloth, like sweat. One wears a dry cloth. Which will cool faster? Guess first.

good: When I come out of the bath I feel cold.
The fan dries the wet one.

flow.context: This is the first step of the sweaty tumbler test. You find out whether being wet, like sweaty skin, helps something cool down.

flow.do: 1. Pour the same amount of warm water into both tumblers, about three-quarters full. 2. Measure the warmth of each with the thermometer. 3. Write both numbers next to 0 minutes.
flow.say: First we measure where we start. Both should be nearly the same. We write them down next to zero minutes.
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to pour the warm water. Measure each tumbler with the thermometer. Write the numbers next to 0 minutes.
flow.parent: Aim for about 40 degrees, comfortably warm, like a body or a bath. If they differ by a degree, that is fine. Write it down anyway.
flow.context: This is a step of the sweaty tumbler test. You measure how warm the water is at the start.

flow.do: 1. Wet one hanky in tap water and squeeze it until it stops dripping. 2. Wrap it around one tumbler. 3. Wrap the dry hanky around the other. 4. Put both in front of the fan, the same distance away. Switch the fan on.
flow.say: This wet cloth is like sweat on your skin. The dry cloth is like dry skin. The fan is like a breeze.
flow.kid: Wet one cloth and squeeze it. Wrap it round one tumbler. Wrap the dry cloth round the other. Put both by the fan.
flow.context: This is a step of the sweaty tumbler test. You wrap the tumblers and put them by the fan.

flow.do: Every 5 minutes, measure each tumbler and write the numbers in the table. Do this at 5, 10, 15 and 20 minutes.
flow.say: Every 5 minutes, let's measure both. Which one is dropping faster?
flow.kid: Every 5 minutes, measure both tumblers. Write the numbers. Which one is cooling faster?
flow.parent: Put the thermometer in the water each time and wait until the number stops changing. Wipe it between tumblers. While you wait, touch both cloths. The wet one feels cold. A fever thermometer will not do, because most cannot read below about 32 degrees. On a humid monsoon day the difference is smaller, but it is still there. If you have no thermometer, a family member can touch each tumbler with their eyes closed and say which is cooler.
flow.context: This is the measuring part of the sweaty tumbler test. You check both tumblers every 5 minutes.

flow.do: Work out how much each tumbler dropped. Take the 20 minute number away from the 0 minute number.
flow.say: Let's see how much each tumbler cooled. Start number take away end number.
flow.kid: Take the end number away from the start number. That is how much each tumbler cooled.

check.q: In the sweaty tumbler test, the wet cloth tumbler cooled more. Why?
options: The water drying from the cloth carried heat away
Wet cloth is made of colder cotton
check.why: As the water in the cloth evaporates into the moving air, the fastest water molecules fly off and take heat with them. That cools the tumbler. Picking 'colder cotton' usually means thinking wet things are cold by themselves. But the cloth was wetted with room-warm water. It got cold because it was drying. Picking 'the dry cloth made heat' mixes up keeping heat in with making heat.

flow.context: This is a step of the sweaty tumbler test. You work out which tumbler cooled more.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three things: what I think, what I saw, and why.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. A good answer: What I think: being wet helps you cool down. What I saw: the wet cloth tumbler went from 40 to 31 degrees, and the dry one only went from 40 to 37. Why: the water dried in the fan's breeze and carried heat away. That is how sweat cools me.
flow.think: What do you think would happen on a sticky, humid monsoon day, when the wet cloth dries slowly?
flow.context: This is the last step of the sweaty tumbler test. You explain what you found.

experiments.title: My Steady Inside: does running change my temperature?
experiments.context: In this experiment you take your own temperature under your arm at rest, after running, and after cooling down. You find out how steady your inside stays, compared to how your skin feels.
experiments.question: Does my inside temperature change much when I run around, or does my body keep it steady?
experiments.predict: Guess before you start. After 2 minutes of running on the spot, will your temperature under your arm go up a lot, a little, or not at all? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, measure the same way each time. Use the same thermometer, under the same arm, for the same length of time, until it beeps.
results_table: How my face and hands feel

materials.item: a digital fever thermometer
a clock or timer
a pencil and the results table
a glass of water

experiments.safety: Run on the spot only for 2 minutes, somewhere you cannot slip. Wipe the thermometer with soap and water before and after.

schedule.what: Measure at rest, after 2 minutes of running, and after 10 minutes of rest. Compare.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then circle the biggest and smallest temperatures. How far apart are they?

example_chart.title: Made-up example results
rows: Hot face, red cheeks, a little sweaty

setup.art: A child sitting quietly on a chair with a digital thermometer tucked under one arm.
setup.caption: 1. Sit quietly. Take your temperature under your arm.

setup.art: A child running on the spot on a mat, a timer showing 2 minutes.
setup.caption: 2. Run on the spot for 2 minutes.

setup.art: The same child with red cheeks, taking their temperature again, then resting with a glass of water.
setup.caption: 3. Take your temperature again, then rest 10 minutes and take it once more.

flow.do: 1. Wipe the thermometer. 2. Ask your child to guess how much their temperature will change after running.
flow.say: When you run, your face gets hot and red. But does the inside of your body get hotter too? Let's guess, then measure.
flow.kid: When you run, you feel hot. Does your inside get hotter too? Guess: a lot, a little, or not at all?
flow.context: This is the first step of the My Steady Inside experiment. You measure your own temperature before and after running.

flow.do: 1. Your child sits still for 2 minutes. 2. Tuck the thermometer under their arm, tip in the armpit, arm pressed down. 3. Wait for the beep. 4. Write the number.
flow.say: Sit still. Squeeze your arm gently against your side. We wait for the beep.
flow.kid: Sit still. Put the thermometer tip in your armpit. Squeeze your arm down. Wait for the beep. Write the number.
flow.parent: Under the arm usually reads a little lower than the mouth, around 36 to 37 degrees. Any steady number in that range is normal.
flow.context: This is a step of the My Steady Inside experiment. You take your temperature at rest.

flow.do: 1. Your child runs on the spot for 2 minutes. 2. Straight away, take their temperature again the same way. 3. Ask how their face and hands feel.
flow.say: Run on the spot, as fast as you like, for 2 minutes. Now quickly, thermometer under your arm again. How does your face feel?
flow.kid: Run on the spot for 2 minutes. Then take your temperature again. Touch your face. Is it hot? Are you sweaty?

ask.q: What is your body doing to cool down?
good: My cheeks are red, so blood is near my skin.

flow.context: This is a step of the My Steady Inside experiment. You take your temperature after running.

flow.do: 1. Your child rests for 10 minutes and sips water. Read the story or a card while you wait. 2. Take the temperature once more.
flow.say: Now let's rest and drink some water. In 10 minutes we will measure again.
flow.kid: Rest for 10 minutes. Sip some water. Then take your temperature one more time.
flow.context: This is a step of the My Steady Inside experiment. You rest, then measure again.

flow.do: Look at the three numbers together. Then ask for claim, evidence and reasoning.
flow.say: Your face felt very hot, but your inside only changed a tiny bit. Tell me: what do you think, what did you see, and why?
flow.kid: Look at your three numbers. Say three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.

check.q: After running, your face felt hot, but your temperature under your arm went up by less than one degree. Why?
options: Your body sweated and sent blood to the skin to get rid of the extra heat
Running does not make any heat
check.why: Running makes lots of heat in your muscles. But your body got rid of it fast, by sweating and sending warm blood to your skin. That is homeostasis keeping your inside steady. Picking 'running makes no heat' misses why your face got hot. Picking 'the thermometer was broken' is worth checking, but most children who try this find only a small change.

flow.parent: A good answer: What I think: my body keeps my inside steady. What I saw: my temperature went from 36.5 to 36.8 and back to 36.6, but my face felt very hot. Why: I sweated and my skin got red, so the heat got out.
flow.context: This is the last step of the My Steady Inside experiment. You explain what your numbers show.

experiments.title: The Matka Test: can a pot sweat?
experiments.context: In this experiment you fill a clay matka and a steel pot with the same water, and leave them for a few hours. Then you measure which water is cooler, and feel the outside of each pot.
experiments.question: Does water stay cooler in a clay matka than in a steel pot? And why?
experiments.predict: Guess before you start. After 3 hours, will the matka water be cooler, the same, or warmer than the steel pot water? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, use the same water for both, the same amount, and leave both in the same place, in the shade, side by side.

materials.item: a clay matka, soaked in water for an hour first. If you have no matka, use an unglazed clay kulhad and a steel tumbler of the same size
a steel pot or a big steel bottle
tap water, the same for both
a thermometer
two plates to cover the pots

experiments.safety: Use clean drinking water if anyone will drink it afterwards. A grown-up helps carry the full matka, because it is heavy.

schedule.what: Fill both pots. Measure the start. Wait 3 hours. Measure again and feel the outsides. Explain what you found.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw the matka with little arrows showing water creeping out and drying away.

setup.art: A clay matka and a steel pot side by side in the shade on a verandah, both being filled from one jug.
setup.caption: 1. Fill both pots with the same water. Measure the start.

setup.art: A clock showing 3 hours later, the matka's outside looking darker and damp, the steel pot dry.
setup.caption: 2. Leave both in the shade for 3 hours.

setup.art: A child's hand on the damp, cool side of the matka, a thermometer in the water.
setup.caption: 3. Measure both again. Feel the outside of each pot.

flow.do: 1. Soak the matka in water for an hour beforehand. 2. Fill both pots with the same water. 3. Measure the warmth of each and write it down. 4. Cover both with plates.
flow.say: People say a matka keeps water cool. Is that true, or just a story? Let's test it against a steel pot.
flow.kid: Fill a matka and a steel pot with the same water. Measure each one. Write the numbers. Cover them.
flow.context: This is the first step of the matka test. You find out if a clay pot keeps water cooler than a steel pot.

flow.do: Put both pots in the shade, side by side, where a little breeze blows.
flow.say: Now we wait. The matka has tiny holes we cannot see. Watch what its outside looks like later.
flow.kid: Put both pots in the shade. Now wait 3 hours.
flow.context: This is a step of the matka test. You leave the pots to stand.

flow.do: 1. Measure the water in each pot again. 2. Feel the outside of each pot. 3. Write everything down.
flow.say: Let's measure again. Now feel the outside of the matka. Feel the steel pot. What do you notice?
flow.kid: Measure each pot again. Then feel the outside of each. Which one feels cool and damp?

ask.q: Why is the outside of the matka damp?

flow.parent: On a dry, warm day the matka water is often several degrees cooler than the steel pot water. On a very humid day, the difference is small. That is a great result too, because it shows drying is the key.
flow.context: This is the measuring step of the matka test. You check both pots after 3 hours.

flow.do: Ask for claim, evidence and reasoning. Then compare the matka with sweaty skin.
flow.say: How is the matka like your skin on a hot day? Tell me what you think, what you saw, and why.
flow.kid: How is the matka like your sweaty skin? Say three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.

check.q: In the matka test, the matka water stayed cooler. What is the best reason?
options: Water seeps out and dries on the outside, carrying heat away
The matka was in the shade and the steel pot was in the sun
check.why: The matka's tiny holes let a little water reach the outside. It dries into the air and takes heat with it. That is just like sweat drying on your skin. Picking 'clay is cold' is a common idea, but dry clay in the sun gets very hot. Picking 'shade and sun' would be an unfair test, so in our test both pots stood in the same shade.

flow.think: Mohammed Bah Abba, a teacher in Nigeria, put a clay pot inside a bigger clay pot with wet sand between them. Vegetables kept fresh for many days. Why do you think it worked?
flow.context: This is the last step of the matka test. You explain why the matka keeps water cool.

activities.title: Jump and Notice: what does my body do?

materials.item: a clear space to jump
a mirror
a glass of water

activities.safety: Jump on a mat or a non-slip floor. Stop if you feel dizzy.

schedule.what: Jump for one minute, notice the body's changes, then rest and notice again.

activities.record: Draw yourself before and after jumping. Label everything that changed.
activities.context: This is a short noticing activity. You jump for one minute and then watch what your body does by itself.

setup.art: A child doing star jumps on a mat in a living room.
setup.caption: 1. Jump for one minute.

setup.art: The child looking in a mirror at red cheeks and a shiny forehead.
setup.caption: 2. Look in the mirror. Notice what has changed.

setup.art: The child resting on the floor with a glass of water, looking calm.
setup.caption: 3. Rest and sip water. Notice what changes back.

flow.do: 1. Your child looks in a mirror and touches their face and hands. 2. Then they do star jumps for one minute while you time it.
flow.say: Look at your face in the mirror. Touch your cheeks. Now jump as fast as you can for one minute. I'll time you.
flow.kid: Look at your face in the mirror. Touch your cheeks. Now jump for one minute!
flow.context: This is the first step of Jump and Notice. You jump, then notice what your body does without being told.

flow.do: Straight after jumping, look in the mirror again. Ask what they notice and what they wonder.
flow.say: Look now! What do you notice about your face, your skin and your breathing? What do you wonder?
flow.kid: Look in the mirror. What do you notice? Red cheeks? Sweat? Fast breathing? Are you thirsty?

good: Who told my body to do that?

flow.parent: Write down every 'I wonder'. The rest of the unit answers them. Do not explain yet.
flow.context: This is a step of Jump and Notice. You look at what your body did by itself after jumping.

flow.do: Your child rests and sips water for 3 minutes. Then they look in the mirror one more time.
flow.say: Now rest and sip water. Did anything go back to normal? Did you decide to sweat, or did your body do it by itself?
flow.kid: Rest and sip water. Look again. What went back to normal? Did you choose to sweat?

check.q: After jumping, your face went red and sweaty. Who made that happen?
options: My body did it by itself, to cool me down
The mirror made my face red
check.why: Your body sweats and sends blood to your skin by itself, without you choosing. A part of your brain does it to cool you down. Picking 'I decided' is a good guess, because it is your body. But try to sweat right now, on purpose. You can't! That shows a hidden part of you is in charge.

flow.think: If you didn't choose to sweat, who did?
flow.context: This is the last step of Jump and Notice. You see your body going back to normal.

activities.title: Cold Hands, Warm Hands

materials.item: a steel bowl of cold tap water with 4 or 5 ice cubes
a bowl of comfortably warm water
a towel

activities.safety: Keep a hand in the cold water for one minute at most, and take it out sooner if it hurts. A grown-up checks the warm water is not hot.

schedule.what: Make one hand cold. Press a fingertip on each hand and count how long the colour takes to come back. Then warm the cold hand and try again.

activities.record: Write down how many seconds the colour took to come back on the cold hand, the other hand, and the warmed hand.
activities.context: This activity shows how your blood vessels squeeze narrow in the cold to keep heat in. You see it in how slowly the pink colour comes back after you press your skin.

setup.art: A child dipping one hand into a steel bowl of water with ice cubes floating.
setup.caption: 1. Put one hand in cold water for one minute.

setup.art: A thumb pressing the pad of a fingertip, leaving a small white spot that slowly turns pink.
setup.caption: 2. Press a fingertip for 3 seconds. Count until it is pink again.

setup.art: The cold hand resting in a bowl of warm water, the fingertips pink again.
setup.caption: 3. Warm the cold hand and test it again.

flow.do: 1. Your child presses the pad of a finger on their dry hand for 3 seconds, then lets go. 2. Count the seconds until the white spot is pink again. 3. Now they put the other hand in the cold water for one minute, then dry it.
flow.say: Press your fingertip hard for three seconds and let go. See the white spot? Let's count until it is pink again. Now put your other hand in the cold water for one minute.
flow.kid: Press a fingertip for 3 seconds. Let go. Count until it is pink. Then put your other hand in cold water.
flow.parent: On a warm hand the colour usually comes back in about 1 or 2 seconds. Count out loud: one thousand, two thousand.
flow.context: This is the first step of Cold Hands, Warm Hands. You time how fast colour comes back to a warm fingertip, then make the other hand cold.

flow.do: 1. Press a fingertip of the cold hand for 3 seconds and let go. 2. Count until it is pink again. 3. Ask your child why it is slower.
flow.say: Now the cold hand. Press, let go, and count. Was it slower? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Press a cold fingertip. Let go. Count. Is it slower this time?

ask.q: Why do you think the colour came back more slowly?
good: Less blood is going to the cold hand.

flow.parent: The cold fingertip usually takes clearly longer to turn pink. A cold hand may look pinker or blotchy rather than pale, and that is fine. The slow return of colour is what to look at. After your child has guessed, explain: in the cold, the tiny blood vessels in the skin squeeze narrow. Less warm blood flows there, so less heat escapes, and your body keeps its heat for your middle.

check.q: In Cold Hands, Warm Hands, the cold fingertip took longer to turn pink after you pressed it. Why?
options: The blood vessels in the cold skin had squeezed narrow, so less blood flowed there
The cold water washed the colour off
The cold hand had no blood at all
check.why: In the cold, the tiny blood vessels in your skin squeeze narrow. Less warm blood flows near the skin, so less heat escapes. That also means blood refills a pressed spot more slowly. Picking 'washed the colour off' means thinking skin colour sits on top, but the pink comes from blood underneath. Your hand always has blood, just less near the surface when it is cold.

flow.context: This is a step of Cold Hands, Warm Hands. You find out why colour comes back slowly to a cold fingertip.

flow.do: Your child puts the cold hand in the warm water for one minute, dries it, and does the press test again.
flow.say: Now warm it up for a minute. Press and count again. Is it fast again? The blood vessels have opened wide, so warm blood comes back quickly.
flow.kid: Put the cold hand in warm water. Press a fingertip again. Count. Is it fast now?
flow.think: Why do you think your cheeks go red when you run, and your fingers go cold in winter?
flow.context: This is the last step of Cold Hands, Warm Hands. You watch the blood come back.

activities.title: Thermostat Hunt

materials.item: sticky notes or small paper slips
a pencil

activities.safety: Do not touch the iron, geyser or stove. Only look, and ask a grown-up how they work.

schedule.what: Hunt around the house for machines that keep something just right. Label each one.

activities.record: Draw one machine's feedback loop: what notices, what decides, what acts.
activities.context: In this activity you hunt for machines at home that keep something just right, the way your body does. Each one has a feedback loop.

setup.art: A child sticking a paper slip on a fridge door that says 'keeps it cold'.
setup.caption: 1. Find machines that keep something just right.

setup.art: Sticky notes on an AC, an iron and a water tank float, each with a small arrow loop drawn.
setup.caption: 2. Label each one with what it keeps steady.

setup.art: A child's drawing of a loop: thermometer, then a little box 'decides', then a fan 'acts', with an arrow back.
setup.caption: 3. Draw one machine's loop.

flow.do: Walk around the house together. Look for the fridge, AC, geyser, iron, overhead tank float and pressure cooker.
flow.say: Your body keeps itself just right. Some machines at home do this too. Let's find them. For each one, what does it keep steady?
flow.kid: Hunt around your home. Find machines that keep something just right. Stick a note on each. What does it keep steady?
flow.parent: The fridge keeps cold. The AC and geyser keep warmth. The iron has a dial and a light that switches off when hot enough. The overhead tank's float valve shuts the water off when full. The pressure cooker whistle lets steam out when the pressure gets too high.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Thermostat Hunt. You look for machines that keep something steady, like your body does.

flow.do: Pick one machine. Ask your child to draw its loop: what notices, what decides, what acts.
flow.say: Let's draw the AC's loop. What notices that the room is too warm? What decides? What acts? And how is your body the same?
flow.kid: Pick one machine. Draw its loop. What notices? What decides? What acts? Now draw your body's loop for sweating.

check.q: In your body's sweating loop, what is the 'decider', like the AC's control box?
options: The hypothalamus, a small part of your brain
check.why: The hypothalamus compares your warmth with 'just right' and decides what to do. Sweat glands are the actors: they do what the brain decides. Picking sweat glands is close, because they are part of the loop. Their job in this loop is to act on the brain's message.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Thermostat Hunt. You draw a feedback loop for a machine and for your body.

activities.title: The Body Council

materials.item: paper and pens for name signs
soft toys to play the sensors
a glass of water and a towel as props

schedule.what: Act out the body's council: sensors report, the Brain Mayor decides, the teams act.

activities.record: Write down the best scene. Who noticed, who decided, who acted?
activities.context: The Body Council is a play. The child is the Brain Mayor. Soft toys are the sensors, and the grown-up plays the Sweat Team, the Shiver Team and the Thirst Team.

setup.art: A child wearing a paper crown labelled 'Brain Mayor', soft toys labelled 'Skin sensor' lined up in front.
setup.caption: 1. Make name signs. The child is the Brain Mayor.

setup.art: A parent pretending to wipe sweat as the 'Sweat Team' while the child points like a mayor.
setup.caption: 2. The sensors report, the mayor decides, the team acts.

flow.do: Make signs: Brain Mayor, Skin Sensor, Salt Sensor, Sweat Team, Shiver Team, Thirst Team. Give the child the mayor's crown.
flow.say: You are the Brain Mayor. These toys are your sensors. I am all your teams. When a sensor reports a problem, you decide which team to send.
flow.kid: You are the Brain Mayor. The toys are sensors. The grown-up plays the teams. You decide who to send.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Body Council play. You set up the characters of your body's balance team.

flow.do: Play scenes. Make the toy sensors 'report': 'Too hot in the kitchen!', 'Cold wind!', 'The blood is getting salty!'. The mayor decides. You act the team.
flow.say: Skin Sensor reporting, Mayor! It is too hot in the kitchen! What do you order? ... Sweat Team on the way! Now the sensor says it is just right. What do you order now?
flow.kid: Listen to the sensors. Decide which team to send. When things are just right again, tell the team to stop.

ask.q: Why does the mayor have to tell the team to stop?
good: Or you would get too cold.

check.q: In the Body Council play, the Salt Sensor says 'The blood is too salty!' Which team does the mayor send?
check.why: Salty blood means too little water. Feeling thirsty makes you drink, which adds water back. Sending the Sweat Team would make it worse, because sweating loses water. Sending the Shiver Team is for cold, not for water.

flow.context: This is the main part of the Body Council play. The Brain Mayor decides which team to send.

activities.title: Goosebump Watch

materials.item: a magnifying glass, if you have one. Your eyes alone are enough.
a damp cloth
a fan

activities.safety: Use the fan on a gentle setting. Keep fingers away from the blades.

schedule.what: Make a patch of arm skin cool and watch the hairs stand up under a magnifying glass.

activities.record: Draw your arm skin before and after, as you saw it through the magnifying glass.
activities.context: In this activity you watch goosebumps appear up close. You find out what they are, and why furry animals have a better use for them than we do.

setup.art: A child looking at the hairs on their forearm through a magnifying glass.
setup.caption: 1. Look at the hairs on your arm.

setup.art: A damp cloth wiping the forearm, then the arm held in front of a gentle fan.
setup.caption: 2. Wipe your arm with a damp cloth and hold it by the fan.

setup.art: A close-up of goosebumps with hairs standing straight up.
setup.caption: 3. Look again. Watch for goosebumps.

flow.do: 1. Look at the arm through the magnifying glass. 2. Wipe the arm with a damp cloth. 3. Hold it in front of the fan for 30 seconds. 4. Look again.
flow.say: Look closely at the little hairs on your arm. Now let's make it cold. Look again. What has changed?
flow.kid: Look at your arm hairs through the glass. Wipe your arm with a damp cloth. Hold it by the fan. Look again!
flow.context: This is the first step of Goosebump Watch. You make your arm cool and look for goosebumps.
flow.parent: If no goosebumps come on a hot day, hold a cold steel tumbler from the fridge against the arm for a few seconds, or try after a bath.

flow.do: Explain goosebumps, and compare with a cat fluffing its fur.
flow.say: Each hair has a tiny muscle. When you are cold, it pulls the hair upright. A cat or a monkey has thick fur. Its standing fur traps a blanket of warm air. Our hair is too thin for that. So goosebumps are a leftover from our furry relatives.
flow.kid: Each hair has a tiny muscle. Cold makes it pull the hair up. Furry animals trap warm air this way. Our hair is too thin. Goosebumps are a leftover!

check.q: Why does a cat fluff up its fur on a cold morning?
options: Standing fur traps a layer of warm air
To look bigger to the cold
check.why: Standing fur holds still air, and still air keeps heat in, like a blanket. Cats do also puff up to look bigger when frightened, but on a cold morning it is about warmth. Fur does not make heat. It only keeps in the heat the body makes.

flow.think: When else do you get goosebumps, even when you are not cold?
flow.context: This is the last step of Goosebump Watch. You find out what goosebumps are for.

projects.title: My Water Diary
projects.context: In this 3-day project you keep a diary of your body's water balance. You count your drinks, rate your thirst, and check your pee colour against a chart.

materials.item: a printed diary page for each day
a steel tumbler to count cups
a pee colour chart, drawn with 5 shades from very pale yellow to dark yellow
coloured pencils

projects.safety: Wash your hands after the toilet, as always. If pee is very dark for a whole day, or red or brown, tell a grown-up, who may ask a doctor.

schedule.what: Make the pee colour chart and the diary page. Start counting cups and noting thirst.
Keep the diary. Try a hot or active day, like playing outside.
Finish the diary. Add up the cups for each day. Make a bar chart. Explain what you found.

projects.record: Each day, tally your cups of water and other drinks, rate your thirst from 1 to 5 three times, and colour the pee shade you see. On day 3, draw a bar chart of cups each day.

setup.caption: 1. Make a pee colour chart with 5 shades.

setup.caption: 2. Each day, tally your cups and note your thirst and pee colour.

flow.do: 1. Help your child draw a 5-shade pee colour chart. 2. Draw a diary page with a tally box, a thirst row and a colour box. 3. Start the diary today.
flow.say: Your body keeps its water just right. Thirst tells you to drink, and your kidneys decide how much water to let go as pee. Pee colour is like a message. Pale means plenty of water. Dark means drink more.
flow.kid: Draw 5 shades of yellow, pale to dark. That is your pee chart. Make a diary page. Each drink, make a tally mark.
flow.context: This is day 1 of My Water Diary. You make a chart and start counting your drinks.

flow.do: Keep the diary all day. Try to include some outdoor play.
flow.say: Today let's play outside for a while. Do you think you will drink more or less today? Will your pee be paler or darker?
flow.kid: Keep your diary today. Play outside too. Do you drink more on an active day?
flow.wait: Day 2: keep the diary all day
flow.context: This is day 2 of My Water Diary. You keep counting, on a busier day.

flow.do: 1. Add up each day's cups. 2. Draw a bar for each day. 3. Ask for claim, evidence and reasoning.
flow.say: Let's add up your cups and draw a bar for each day. Which day did you drink most? What was your pee colour that day? What was the weather?
flow.kid: Add up your cups for each day. Draw a bar for each day. Which day did you drink most? Why?

check.q: In your water diary, on the day you played outside in the heat, you felt thirstier and drank more. Why?
options: You lost more water in sweat, so your body asked for more
Playing outside makes your tummy bigger
check.why: On a hot, active day you sweat out more water. Your blood gets a little saltier, and your brain makes you feel thirsty. Drinking puts the water back. That is a feedback loop. Thirst is not random. It follows what your body has lost.

flow.parent: A good answer: What I think: my body asks for more water when I sweat. What I saw: on day 2 I played outside, I drank 8 cups, and I was thirsty three times. On day 1 I drank 5. Why: I lost water in sweat and my body wanted it back.
flow.context: This is the last day of My Water Diary. You add up your cups and explain the pattern.

challenges.title: Cool the Shoebox Room, No Electricity
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. A shoebox stands in the sun like a little room. Your job is to keep the inside as cool as you can, without using electricity.
challenges.problem: Two shoeboxes stand in the sun, on a sunny windowsill or balcony. One is your test room, one stays plain. Make your room's inside as many degrees cooler than the plain box as you can, in 30 minutes.
constraints: No electricity, no ice and no fridge.
You may only use things from home.
Measure the inside of both boxes with a thermometer at the end.
materials: two shoeboxes with a small window cut in one side
a thermometer. With only one, move it from box to box and leave it inside for 2 minutes before you read it.
cotton cloth, water, a spray bottle, white paper, foil, a clay saucer or kulhad
general: Cover the box with white paper or foil, so it reflects sunlight.
Shade it with cardboard or cloth.
Hang a wet cloth over the window, so the air coming in is cooled by drying water.
creative: People in India have hung wet khus grass mats in doorways for hundreds of years. The breeze through the wet mat cools the room. Could you make a tiny one?
Put a damp clay saucer inside, like a tiny matka. Does it help?
Make your box sweat: spray its outside with water every 5 minutes, like skin sweating.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own idea. Draw it, build it, and measure. Did it beat the others? Would it work on a humid monsoon day?

setup.art: Two shoeboxes on a sunny ledge, each with a little window and a thermometer inside.
setup.caption: 1. Put two shoeboxes in the sun with a thermometer in each.

setup.art: One shoebox covered in white paper with a damp cotton curtain over its window, a child spraying it with water.
setup.caption: 2. Change one box to keep it cool.

flow.do: 1. Put both shoeboxes in the sun. 2. Put a thermometer inside each one. 3. Write down the starting numbers.
flow.say: Here are two little rooms in the sun. In 30 minutes, which will be cooler inside? Let's make one of them cool, without any electricity.
flow.kid: Put both boxes in the sun. Put a thermometer in each. Write the numbers.
flow.context: This is the first step of the shoebox room challenge. You set up two boxes in the sun.

flow.do: Your child chooses and builds their cooling ideas on one box only.
flow.say: Think about how your body cools down. Which of those tricks could work for a box?
flow.kid: How does your body cool down? Shade, sweat, red skin? Use one idea on your box.

ask.q: Which of your body's tricks are you copying?
good: Reflecting the sun, like wearing white.

flow.context: This is the building step of the shoebox room challenge. You use your body's cooling tricks on a box.

flow.do: After 30 minutes in the sun, read both thermometers. Compare.
flow.say: Let's read both. How many degrees cooler is your room? Which idea worked best?
flow.kid: Read both thermometers. How much cooler is your box? Which idea helped most?

check.q: In the shoebox challenge, the box with a wet cloth window was coolest. What did the wet cloth copy from your body?
options: Sweating: water drying takes heat away
check.why: The wet cloth dries in the air, and drying takes heat away, just like sweat on skin. Shivering and goosebumps are the body's ways to stay warm, not cool.

flow.context: This is the last step of the shoebox room challenge. You measure which box stayed coolest.

challenges.title: Design a Suit for Another World
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You design a suit that keeps a person at just right, 37 degrees inside, on a freezing moon or on a blazing hot planet.
challenges.problem: An explorer must walk for one hour on a world that is either far too cold or far too hot. Design a suit that keeps their body just right inside.
constraints: The explorer must be able to move and see.
The suit must deal with sweat and body heat, as well as the outside.
Draw the suit, label every part, and say which body trick each part copies.
materials: scraps of cloth, foil, cotton wool, plastic straws, tape
general: For cold: thick layers that trap still air, like fur or a shawl.
For heat: shiny or white outside to reflect sunlight, and loose cloth.
Gloves and boots, because fingers and toes lose heat first.
creative: Real astronauts wear a cooling suit under their spacesuit. It has thin tubes with cool water flowing through them, carrying body heat away. Could your suit have tubes made of straws?
Penguins huddle together in winter, and take turns at the cold outside of the group. Could a team of explorers do the same?
A camel's thick hair on its back keeps the desert sun off. Could your hot-planet suit copy that?
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own suit. Build a small version on a doll. Explain each part to someone at home.

setup.art: A child drawing a spacesuit on paper with labels like 'layers trap air' and 'shiny outside'.
setup.caption: 1. Choose a cold world or a hot world. Draw your suit.

setup.art: A small doll dressed in a foil cape and cotton wool layers, with straws taped along its arms.
setup.caption: 2. Build a small version on a doll.

setup.art: A child pointing to the parts of the doll suit while explaining to a parent.
setup.caption: 3. Explain which body trick each part copies.

flow.do: Your child picks a cold world or a hot world and draws a suit, labelling each part.
flow.say: Your explorer is about 37 degrees inside, just like you. How will your suit keep them just right out there?
flow.kid: Choose a cold world or a hot world. Draw a suit. Label each part.
flow.context: This is the first step of the suit design challenge. You plan a suit that keeps an explorer just right.

flow.do: Build a small version on a doll, using the scraps.
flow.say: Let's make a small suit for this doll. Which parts are the most important?
flow.kid: Build a small suit on a doll. Use foil, cotton wool and straws.
flow.context: This is the building step of the suit design challenge.

flow.do: Your child explains the suit and which body trick each part copies.
flow.say: Tell me about each part of your suit. Which body trick does it copy?
flow.kid: Explain each part of your suit. Which body trick is it copying?

check.q: In the suit design challenge, an explorer on a hot planet is sweating inside a closed suit. Why might they still overheat?
options: The sweat cannot dry inside the closed suit, so it does not cool them
Closed suits are always cold inside
check.why: Sweat only cools when it dries. Inside a closed suit the air gets damp, like a monsoon day, and sweat stops drying. That is why real astronauts need cooling water tubes. Sweat does not make heat. Closed suits trap the body's own heat, so they get warm, not cold.

flow.context: This is the last step of the suit design challenge. You explain how your suit keeps the explorer just right.

opts: The body keeping its inside steady and just right
quiz.why: Homeostasis means keeping things like warmth and water just right inside. Picking 'growing' mixes it up with change.

quiz.p: About how warm is the inside of a healthy body?
opts: As warm as the weather outside
quiz.why: About 37 degrees. Picking 'as warm as the weather' comes from how our skin feels, but the inside stays steady.

opts: It dries and carries heat away
It is cold when it comes out
quiz.why: Sweat comes out warm. It cools you when it evaporates. Picking 'cold when it comes out' is the most common mix-up.
Working muscles make heat. Picking 'cools you down' mixes up shivering with sweating.

quiz.p: Why do you feel thirsty after playing in the sun?
opts: You lost water in sweat, and your brain noticed
quiz.why: Sweat takes water out of you. Your blood gets a little saltier, and the hypothalamus makes you feel thirsty. Picking 'tummy is empty' mixes up thirst with hunger.

opts: You need to drink more water
quiz.why: When you are low on water, your kidneys save it, so your pee is smaller in amount and darker. Picking 'drank too much' is the opposite: lots of water makes pee pale.

quiz.p: In a feedback loop, what happens after the body acts?
opts: It checks again, and stops when things are just right
quiz.why: A feedback loop checks again. If you kept sweating for ever, you would get too cold and lose too much water.

quiz.p: Which part of you is the 'decider' for sweating and shivering?
quiz.why: The hypothalamus compares your warmth with the set point and decides. Sweat glands act on the brain's message.

quiz.p: Remember the sweaty tumbler test, with a wet cloth and a dry cloth on two tumblers of warm water by a fan? Why did we use the same tumblers and the same water?
opts: To make it a fair test, so only the wet cloth was different
quiz.why: In a fair test, you change only one thing. Then you know that thing caused the difference. Here, it was the wet cloth.

quiz.p: Remember the sweaty tumbler test? The wet tumbler dropped 9 degrees and the dry one dropped 3 degrees. Which is true?
opts: The wet one cooled 3 times as much
quiz.why: 9 divided by 3 is 3. So the wet one cooled 3 times as much. Drying water carried heat away.

chart.title: How many degrees each tumbler cooled in 20 minutes

quiz.p: How does an elephant cool down?
opts: It flaps its big ears, which are full of blood vessels
quiz.why: Moving air over the ears cools the blood flowing through them. Shivering and fur are for keeping warm.

quiz.p: Which machine works like your body's warmth loop?
quiz.why: An AC notices, compares with its set number, and acts. A spoon, pencil or ball cannot notice and correct anything.

quiz.p: Which of these do scientists still NOT know for sure?
opts: Why our just-right number is about 37 degrees
That sweat cools us by drying
quiz.why: The other three are well tested. Why 37 is still an open question, with ideas like keeping fungi out.

quiz.p: Why is a very humid heatwave more dangerous than a dry one at the same temperature?
opts: Sweat cannot dry well, so the body cannot cool itself
quiz.why: Sweat cools only by drying. In very humid air it hardly dries, so the body heats up. Scientists are still working out exactly where the danger limit is.

quiz.p: A cup of hot chai cools to the warmth of the room, but you don't. Why?
opts: Your body keeps using food to make heat and keep balance
quiz.why: Living things use energy all the time to stay just right. Without it, a body would drift to the room's warmth, like the chai.

applications: Doctors use a thermometer to check for fever, when the body's set point has moved up.
ORS packets put back water and salt for people with loose motions, cholera or heat exhaustion.
Heat action plans, like the one started in Ahmedabad in 2013, warn people, open cool shelters and give out water during heatwaves.
Clay matkas and surahis cool drinking water without electricity.
Desert coolers blow air through wet pads, using the same trick as sweat.
ACs, fridges, geysers and irons use thermostats, which are feedback loops.
Cricketers and athletes plan drinks breaks and cooling towels in hot matches.
Astronauts wear a suit of thin water tubes under their spacesuit, to carry body heat away.
Newborn babies in hospital are kept in warm cots or held skin to skin, because they lose heat quickly.
Builders and farmers are told to work early and late in the day in summer, and rest in the shade at noon.
Engineers design buildings with shade, thick walls and courtyards to stay cool, like old havelis in Rajasthan.

open_questions.q: Why did mammals end up at about 37 degrees, and birds at about 40?
open_questions.why_open: There are ideas, like keeping fungi out, but no test can rewind evolution to check.

open_questions.q: Exactly how hot and humid can it get before healthy people cannot survive?
open_questions.why_open: It is hard and unsafe to test on people. Different studies give different limits, and it depends on age, health and work.

open_questions.q: How does the brain choose its set points, and move them, as in a fever?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know some of the brain cells involved, but not the full picture of how they work together.

open_questions.q: Why do we feel thirst and cold as feelings, and not just fix them without noticing?
open_questions.why_open: This is part of the big puzzle of how the brain makes feelings at all. Nobody knows.

open_questions.q: Is the whole Earth a self-balancing system, and how strong are its balancing loops?
open_questions.why_open: The Earth is hard to experiment on, and its slow loops take thousands of years.

open_questions.q: Why has normal body temperature dropped over the last 150 years?
open_questions.why_open: Some scientists think it is less illness and warmer homes. Others think it is how temperatures were measured. Old data cannot be re-measured.

maths.problem: In the sweaty tumbler test, both tumblers started at 40 degrees. After 20 minutes, the wet cloth tumbler was 31 degrees. The dry cloth tumbler was 37 degrees. How many degrees did each one cool? How many times as much did the wet one cool?
maths.answer: The wet one cooled 9 degrees. The dry one cooled 3 degrees. The wet one cooled 3 times as much.
maths.explain: 40 take away 31 is 9. 40 take away 37 is 3. 9 divided by 3 is 3. You can check: 3 + 3 + 3 = 9.
maths.context: This is about the sweaty tumbler test. You put two tumblers of warm water by a fan, one wrapped in a wet cloth and one in a dry cloth, and measured them.

chart.title: How many degrees each tumbler cooled in 20 minutes

maths.why_maths: Scientists don't just say 'the wet one cooled more'. Taking away tells us how much each cooled, and dividing tells us how many times more.

maths.problem: Look at this thermometer. It was under a child's arm in the My Steady Inside test. The scale goes up in steps of half a degree. What does it read?
maths.explain: The line stops at the big mark labelled 37. The small marks on either side are 36 and a half, and 37 and a half. So it reads 37 degrees, which is normal.
maths.context: This is about the My Steady Inside test, where you took your temperature under your arm before and after running.

chart.title: A body thermometer, in degrees Celsius
chart.label: Read where the line stops.

maths.why_maths: A thermometer is a number line. Reading it carefully is how we know whether a body is just right or has a fever.

maths.problem: In My Water Diary, a child drank 5 cups on day 1, 8 cups on day 2 when they played outside, and 6 cups on day 3. Each cup holds 200 millilitres. How many cups did they drink in all? How many millilitres did they drink on day 2?
maths.answer: 19 cups in all. 1,600 millilitres on day 2.
maths.explain: 5 + 8 + 6 = 19 cups. On day 2, 8 cups of 200 millilitres each is 8 times 200, which is 1,600 millilitres. That is a little more than one and a half litres.
maths.context: This is about My Water Diary, the 3-day project where you tallied every cup you drank.

chart.title: Cups of water and other drinks each day

maths.why_maths: Counting and adding your cups turns a feeling, 'I was thirsty', into numbers you can compare across days.

maths.problem: In Keep It Just Right, your counter starts on box 5. You draw 'Played cricket at noon: +2', then 'Drank hot chai: +1'. Which box are you on? How many do you need to take away to get back to 5, and which body cards add up to that?
maths.answer: Box 8. You need to take away 3. Sweat (minus 2) and Red cheeks (minus 1) add up to 3.
maths.explain: 5 + 2 = 7. 7 + 1 = 8. To get from 8 to 5 you need to take away 3. Sweat takes away 2, which leaves you on 6. Red cheeks take away 1 more, and that brings you to 5. In the game you play one card a turn, so it takes two turns.
maths.context: This is about Keep It Just Right, the card game where event cards push your warmth dial up or down, and body cards bring it back to 5.
maths.why_maths: Your body is always solving a missing number problem: how much do I need to change to get back to just right?

roots.context: We have been learning how the body keeps itself just right, by sweating, shivering and feeling thirsty. Now we ask what this steady balance tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: After jumping, your cheeks turned red. You did not decide to do that. A small part of your brain felt the heat and opened up the blood vessels in your skin. So your body checks and corrects its own warmth all day, without asking you.
deep_truth.habit: We think of 'me' as the one who runs our body, because we choose to walk, eat and talk. But our warmth is kept by a loop that works without our noticing: sensors notice, the hypothalamus compares with about 37 degrees, and skin and muscles act.
deep_truth.evidence: In Jump and Notice, your cheeks went red and you could not sweat on purpose. In My Steady Inside, your face felt hot after running, but the thermometer under your arm rose less than one degree.

three.who_am_i: You are a body that keeps itself near 37 degrees, every minute. Most of that work is done by parts of you that work without you noticing.
three.what_is_life: Every living thing keeps its inside just right while the outside changes. A cell, a beehive and a lotus flower all do it.
three.what_is_this_world: Your heat and water leave you all the time, into the air of the room. Food and drink from the world bring them back.

roots.thread: The same loop keeps balance at every size. One cell pumps salt to keep its inside right. Your hypothalamus keeps your whole body near 37 degrees. Honeybees fan their wings to keep their hive near 35 degrees. Each one notices a change and acts to undo it, so one simple pattern shows up in countless living things.

teachings.teaching: Krishna says that cold and heat, pleasure and pain, come from the senses touching the world. They come and go. They do not last. Learn to bear them steadily.
teachings.link: The Gita is talking about the mind, not body warmth. But it uses the same example: heat and cold come and go, and something in you can stay steady while they do.

teachings.source: Anguttara Nikaya 6.55, the Buddha's teaching to Sona
teachings.teaching: Sona, a monk who used to play the vina, was trying far too hard. The Buddha asked him: if the strings are too tight, does the vina play well? If they are too loose? Only strings tuned just right make music. Balance your effort the same way.
teachings.link: Your body does not aim for as hot as possible or as cold as possible. It aims for just right, and keeps tuning, like a vina.

teachings.teaching: The way of nature is like bending a bow. What is too high is pressed down, and what is too low is lifted up. Where there is too much, it takes away. Where there is too little, it adds.
teachings.link: That is how a feedback loop works. Too hot, and your body cools you. Too cold, and it warms you. Too little water, and you feel thirsty.

science.text: Warming or cooling a tiny spot in the hypothalamus makes an animal pant or shiver, even when the rest of its body is at its normal warmth. That spot works as the body's thermostat.
In mice, thirst cells in the brain switch off within moments of drinking, long before the water reaches the blood. So the brain can correct a change before it has fully happened.

other_view.view: They say the body keeps its balance by chemistry and nerve signals alone, the way a thermostat keeps a room cool. They see no need for any mind in it. Walter Cannon called his 1932 book The Wisdom of the Body, but they say he meant it only as a way of speaking.

practice.title: Cooling breath
practice.say: Let's sit tall and still. Curl your tongue into a little tube, or if you can't, just open your lips a little. Breathe in slowly through your mouth. Feel how cool the air is on your tongue. Now close your mouth and breathe out slowly through your nose. Let's do that five times. Your tongue felt cool because the air was drying it, like sweat on skin. Now just sit and notice. Is your body hot, cold or just right? You didn't have to do anything to stay just right. Who is doing it?
practice.kid: Sit tall. Curl your tongue like a tube. Breathe in slowly through it. Feel the cool. Breathe out through your nose. Do it five times. Then sit still and notice your warmth.

ask: Your hypothalamus decides when you sweat, and you do not notice it deciding. Is that still you deciding?
Who keeps you just right while you sleep?
When your sweat dries into the air, is it still part of you?
A lotus flower keeps itself warm on a cool night. What do you think the flower senses while it does that?
